title: Moving to Costa Rica: A Buyer's Guide to Actually Making the Move
excerpt: The move in the order that actually works: pick the town before the house, rent through a green season, match your title to your residency plan, and know the real carrying costs before you buy.
meta_desc: A step-by-step guide to moving to Costa Rica: choosing your town, renting first, residency paths, real carrying costs, schools, and buying the right property.
body:
**If you are thinking about moving to Costa Rica, or buying property here so you can move later, message me and I will help you think it through.** I am Tiago Leao, an agent with KRAIN in Guanacaste, and my own family made this exact move 15 years ago. You do not need to be ready to buy, ready to move, or ready to do anything except ask a question. [WhatsApp](https://wa.me/50683028660) is the fastest way to reach me and I answer every message myself, in English, Spanish or Portuguese.

The rest of this guide is what I would tell you on that call, written down.

Moving to Costa Rica is really two decisions that people usually collapse into one: where you want your life to be, and what you want to own. Almost everything that goes wrong in a relocation comes from doing the second one before the first. So this walks the move in the order that actually works, from your first exploratory trip to the day you get the keys, with the costs, the timelines, and the mistakes I watch buyers make from the inside.

I grew up in these beach towns and went through the residency process myself as a dependent. Today I spend my days with American and Canadian families doing what my family did, and I have watched enough of these moves land well, and a few land badly, to know where the difference comes from.

## Start by naming what kind of move this is

There are really only three versions of moving to Costa Rica, and each one points at a different property.

**The full-time move.** You are selling or renting out the house back home and living here. Your priorities are the boring ones: water supply, internet reliability, drive time to a good hospital, drive time to school, whether the road floods in October. Ocean view matters less than you think it will after month four.

**The part-time move.** You are here three to six months a year, usually escaping winter, and the house earns when you are not in it. Now rental performance, management, and location convenience become real financial variables. Start with [what vacation rental income actually looks like in Guanacaste](/blog/costa-rica-vacation-rental-income-guanacaste/), because the gap between gross and net surprises almost everyone.

**The investment-first move.** You buy now, rent it out, and move later. This is the most flexible path and it has a genuine advantage: your property can double as your residency qualification if you structure it right from day one.

Say which one you are out loud before you look at a single listing. The answer changes the town, the price band, the property type, and how you take title.

## Choose the region before the house

Costa Rica is small on a map and large in practice. The Caribbean side, the Central Valley, the Southern Zone, and Guanacaste are four different countries as far as your daily life is concerned. I work Guanacaste, so I will be straight about what that means: dry, sunny, beach-town living with a real dry season and a green season, the country's second international airport at Liberia, and the highest concentration of North American families on the coast.

Inside Guanacaste, the towns are not interchangeable either. Tamarindo is the town with everything, restaurants, schools, services, and the noise that comes with them. Playa Grande is quiet, surf-driven, protected. Flamingo, Potrero and Brasilito are the marina and residential corridor. Conchal is resort-anchored and manicured. Nosara is further out, wellness-focused, and a genuinely different drive.

The single most useful thing you can do here is read a comparison rather than a brochure:

- [Guanacaste's beach towns, compared](/blog/guanacaste-gold-coast-towns-guide/)
- [Tamarindo vs. Playa Grande](/blog/tamarindo-vs-playa-grande-real-estate/)
- [Flamingo vs. Conchal vs. Potrero](/blog/flamingo-vs-conchal-vs-potrero-real-estate/)
- [Tamarindo vs. Nosara](/blog/tamarindo-vs-nosara-real-estate/)

Or skip the reading and just ask me. Send me a message on [WhatsApp](https://wa.me/50683028660) with who is moving, roughly what the budget is, and whether there are kids, and I will tell you which two or three of these towns to spend your first trip in and which ones to skip. That is a fifteen-minute conversation and it has saved people entire trips.

## Rent first. Costa Rica gives you 180 days to be sure

Americans and Canadians can enter as tourists and stay up to 180 days. That is half a year to live somewhere before you commit, and very few countries hand you that much runway.

Use it deliberately. Rent in two towns, not one. Be here in September or October, when the green season is at its wettest, not only in February when everything is postcard-perfect. Drive the school run at 7am. Sit in your prospective neighborhood at 9pm on a Saturday and listen. Get the internet speed test at the actual house.

Most of my best client relationships start a year or more before a purchase, with exactly this. I would rather help you rent, and be the person you call fourteen months later, than sell you the wrong house in week two.

## The money picture: what living here actually costs

Two categories, and people usually get the first one right and the second one wrong.

**Cost of living** is genuinely lower than most of the US and Canada in the places that matter: healthcare, property taxes, help around the house, produce, eating locally. It is not lower in the places people forget: imported groceries, cars, electronics, appliances, air conditioning in April, private school tuition, and anything that arrives in a shipping container. Beach-town Guanacaste is also the most expensive part of Costa Rica. Budgets built from a blog post about Atenas or Grecia do not survive contact with Tamarindo.

**Carrying costs on the property** are the part I can be precise about, because they are structural:

- **Property tax: 0.25 percent** of registered value per year. On a $600,000 home that is $1,500. The [full property tax breakdown](/blog/costa-rica-property-taxes-explained/), including the Luxury Home Tax that applies to higher-value homes, is here.
- **HOA and community fees** vary enormously and are the real number to interrogate, especially in gated and resort communities where they can dwarf the tax bill.
- **Insurance, pool and garden service, pest control, and maintenance.** Salt air, humidity and sun are hard on a house. Deferred maintenance here compounds faster than it does in a temperate climate.
- **Closing costs: roughly 3.5 to 4.5 percent** of the purchase price, one time, usually paid by the buyer. See the [closing costs and taxes guide](/blog/costa-rica-closing-costs-taxes/).

If you want the honest carrying-cost math on a specific property rather than a general range, send me the listing on [WhatsApp](https://wa.me/50683028660), whether it is one of mine or not, and I will build the real number with you line by line. That exercise alone has changed which house a few of my clients bought.

## Residency: pick your lane early

You do not need residency to buy property here. Foreigners own titled property outright, in their own name, with the same rights as citizens. But if you are moving, you will want residency eventually, and the category you qualify for should influence how you buy.

- **Pensionado** requires $1,000 a month in lifetime pension income. Social Security and CPP qualify; 401(k) withdrawals do not.
- **Rentista** requires $2,500 a month in guaranteed unearned income, or the cleaner route, a $60,000 deposit in a Costa Rican bank.
- **Inversionista** requires a $150,000 investment, and real estate counts. This is the path most of my clients take, because the purchase they already wanted to make does double duty.

The detail that costs people money: for Inversionista, the property generally needs to be registered in your **personal name**, not a corporation. Corporations are common here for other good reasons. If you decide on the structure after closing, you may be paying to fix it. Tell your attorney your residency plan at the start, not at signing.

The full breakdown, including CAJA, timelines and taxes, is in my [residency guide for property buyers](/blog/costa-rica-residency-property-buyers/).

## Healthcare, honestly

Residents enroll in CAJA, the public system, at roughly 9 to 11 percent of declared income, and it covers a spouse and children under 18 at no extra cost. Most expats I know use CAJA as their backbone and pay out of pocket or carry private insurance for speed and choice, because private care here costs a fraction of US prices.

The relocation-specific question is not "is healthcare good," it is "how far am I from it." In Guanacaste, routine care is local, the regional hospital is in Liberia, and the top private hospitals are in San José. For most families that is fine. If someone in your household has a condition that needs frequent specialist care, drive time to San José belongs in your town decision, not as an afterthought.

## Families: solve school before you solve house

This is the one I feel strongest about. If you have school-age kids, the school decision constrains the house decision, not the other way around. Guanacaste has a real cluster of bilingual and international schools, but seats are finite, calendars differ, and admissions can run months ahead. Families who fall in love with a house 45 minutes from the school they end up choosing regret it every single morning.

Start with my [guide to schools in Guanacaste](/blog/schools-guanacaste-gold-coast-guide/) and the [school profiles](/schools.html), then draw your search radius around the school. If you tell me your kids' ages I can tell you which schools are realistically taking students this year, which is not always what the websites say.

## The logistics nobody puts in the brochure

- **Shipping a container.** Common, taxable, and slower than quoted. Many people ship the sentimental and buy the rest here. Furniture that thrives in humidity is not the furniture in your living room right now.
- **Cars.** Import duties are high and used-car prices reflect it. A vehicle that is unremarkable in Denver is expensive here. Budget accordingly, and buy something with clearance if you are outside a paved development.
- **Pets.** Very doable, with health certificates and airline-specific rules. Start earlier than you think; summer heat embargoes catch people out.
- **Banking.** Opening a local account as a non-resident is possible but paperwork-heavy, and it gets much easier once you have a DIMEX. Most buyers close in dollars through escrow long before they have a local account.
- **Internet.** Fiber has reached most of the developed coast and is genuinely good where it exists. "Most" is doing work in that sentence. If you work remotely, test the speed at the specific house, and ask what the backup is.
- **Driving.** Your foreign license works while your tourist entry is valid. Waze is standard, addresses are descriptive rather than numeric, and one river crossing in October will teach you more about your route than any map.

## Then, and only then, buy the property

Once you know the town, the school, and your residency lane, the purchase itself is refreshingly orderly. Costa Rica has a centralized national registry, closings run through a notary attorney, and funds move through a regulated escrow company.

The sequence:

1. **Offer and negotiation.** Your agent presents and negotiates terms.
2. **Purchase and sale agreement**, with a deposit, commonly around 10 percent, into [escrow](/blog/costa-rica-real-estate-escrow-guide/).
3. **Due diligence**, typically 15 to 30 days. Your attorney examines title and liens, the survey plan, the [water letter](/blog/costa-rica-property-water-letter-guide/), permits and use-of-land. My [due-diligence checklist](/blog/costa-rica-property-due-diligence-checklist/) is what I hand clients.
4. **Closing.** The deed is signed before a notary and recorded in the registry.

Two Costa Rica-specific things to internalize before you shop. First, most transactions are cash, because local financing for foreigners is limited and expensive; many buyers use home equity or a securities-backed line from home when they want leverage. Second, beachfront is not what it looks like: the first 200 meters from the high tide line is the maritime zone, and most of it is concession land rather than title. Read [titled vs. concession beachfront](/blog/titled-vs-concession-beachfront-costa-rica/) before you fall for anything on the sand.

If you are considering building instead of buying, the real constraints are water availability, the permit chain and construction timelines, not the land price. Start with [what it costs to build in Guanacaste](/blog/cost-to-build-house-guanacaste-costa-rica/) and the [land buying checklist](/blog/buying-land-guanacaste-zoning-water-building-checklist/).

## What actually surprises people in year one

Not the bugs, not the Spanish, not the roads. It is these:

- **Everything takes longer.** Permits, deliveries, repairs, bureaucracy. The people who thrive here stop treating this as a problem to solve and start treating it as the price of admission.
- **The green season is real.** May through November, with September and October the heaviest. It is green, lush and quiet, and it is also when things leak and roads wash. Owning here means budgeting for it.
- **Maintenance is not optional.** A house on this coast needs a person who watches it. If you are part-time, property management is a line item, not a luxury.
- **Community is the whole thing.** The families who stay are the ones who joined something in the first six months, the surf group, the school, the volunteer thing, the Tuesday soccer game. The ones who leave are usually the ones who bought a beautiful house and waited for a life to show up.

## A realistic 18-month timeline

1. **Months 1 to 3.** Exploratory trip. Two towns minimum. Meet an agent and an immigration attorney, ask hard questions, buy nothing.
2. **Months 3 to 6.** Choose your residency category. Start gathering and apostilling documents at home, they are typically only valid for six months, so sequence them.
3. **Months 4 to 9.** Rent here for a stretch, ideally including part of the green season. If you have kids, apply to schools now.
4. **Months 6 to 12.** Shop seriously in one or two towns. Offer, escrow, due diligence, close. Structure title to match your residency plan.
5. **Months 9 to 15.** File the residency application. You can remain in the country legally while it processes once filed.
6. **Months 12 to 18.** Move in, ship or buy, enroll in CAJA, get your DIMEX, and start the part that no checklist covers.

Some people compress this to six months. Some take five years. Both are fine. The order is what matters.

## Let's talk about your move

Most of my clients start talking to me long before they are ready to buy, and that is exactly how it should work. The useful conversations happen while you are still deciding, not after you have already fallen for a house.

I grew up here. I went through this process from the inside, with my own family, at an age where I watched every part of it. I live on this coast full time, I work in **English, Spanish and Portuguese**, and I represent buyers across Guanacaste with KRAIN, from Tamarindo through Playa Grande, Flamingo, Brasilito and Conchal.

What you get by reaching out, none of which costs anything and none of which requires you to be a client:

- **A straight answer about which towns fit you.** Not a list of all of them. Two or three, and the reasons, and which ones to skip.
- **The people, not just the properties.** Immigration attorneys, closing attorneys, escrow companies, inspectors, builders, property managers, school contacts. My clients tell me the vetted list is worth more than any listing.
- **Honest carrying-cost math** on any property you are considering, mine or someone else's, including the HOA fee that most listings gloss over.
- **A read on timing.** Whether what you want exists at your number right now, or whether you should wait, rent, or widen the search.
- **Me telling you not to buy something.** Regularly. I would rather lose a transaction than sell a family a house 45 minutes from their school or a beachfront lot that turns out to be concession rather than title.

### The easiest way to start

Send me a WhatsApp message with these four things. It takes a minute to write and it is enough for me to give you something genuinely useful back:

1. **Who is moving** and roughly when.
2. **Your budget range**, even a wide one.
3. **Kids, and their ages**, if any.
4. **What you would be doing here**: retiring, working remotely, renting the place out, or still figuring that out.

I answer every message myself. Not an assistant, not a form, not a drip campaign.

**[Message me on WhatsApp](https://wa.me/50683028660).** You can also find me on [Instagram](https://instagram.com/soldbytiago) or email tiago@soldbytiago.com.

If you are somewhere between "we talk about this on Sunday nights" and "we fly down next month," that is the right time to reach out. And if you would rather read a while longer first, my [Buyer's Guide](/buyers-guide.html) covers the transaction mechanics and [current listings](/properties.html) will calibrate your budget faster than any price article.

*This article is general information, not legal, tax or immigration advice. Immigration categories, tax thresholds and municipal practice change, and every situation differs. Confirm current requirements with a licensed Costa Rican immigration attorney, real estate attorney and accountant before acting. References: [Direccion General de Migracion](https://www.migracion.go.cr), [Ministerio de Hacienda](https://www.hacienda.go.cr), [CCSS](https://www.ccss.sa.cr), [Registro Nacional](https://www.registronacional.go.cr). Cost-of-living observations reflect the Guanacaste coast in 2026 and are my own, not survey data.*

## FAQ

### How much money do you need to move to Costa Rica?

It depends on the residency path and the lifestyle. The formal minimums are $1,000 a month in lifetime pension income for Pensionado, $2,500 a month in unearned income or a $60,000 bank deposit for Rentista, and a $150,000 investment for Inversionista. Beach-town Guanacaste costs meaningfully more to live in than the Central Valley, so budgets built from national averages tend to run short.

### Can I move to Costa Rica without residency?

You can live here on tourist entries of up to 180 days and buy property with full ownership rights, since foreigners have the same property rights as citizens. What you cannot do without residency is enroll in CAJA, work for a Costa Rican company, or stay indefinitely without leaving. Most people who move permanently start on a tourist entry and file for residency within the first year.

### Should I rent or buy first when moving to Costa Rica?

Rent first, almost always. The 180-day tourist entry gives you enough time to live in two towns, experience the green season, and test the school run before committing. The most expensive mistakes I see come from buying in week two of a first visit.

### Is Guanacaste a good place to move with kids?

It is one of the easier parts of Costa Rica for families, because this part of Guanacaste has a cluster of bilingual and international schools and a large established North American community. The practical rule is to choose the school first and then search for a house inside a sane drive of it, since seats are limited and commutes here are longer than the distance suggests.

### What is the biggest mistake people make moving to Costa Rica?

Buying before they have lived here through a green season, and buying without matching the title structure to their residency plan. The first produces a house in the wrong town; the second produces legal work you pay for twice.

## About the author

Tiago Leao is a real estate agent with KRAIN Luxury Real Estate in Guanacaste, working Tamarindo, Playa Grande, Flamingo, Brasilito and Conchal. His family moved to Costa Rica 15 years ago and he went through the residency process himself, which is why relocating buyers make up most of his business. He works in English, Spanish and Portuguese, and builds every signature listing its own dedicated marketing page at [soldbytiago.com/signature/](https://soldbytiago.com/signature/). Reach him on [WhatsApp](https://wa.me/50683028660).

title: Best Places to Live in Costa Rica With Kids: The 2026 Family Guide
excerpt: Hacienda Pinilla, Reserva Conchal, Flamingo and Potrero, and Tamarindo: where families actually settle on the Guanacaste coast, which schools each one is close to, and what to know before you move.
meta_desc: The best areas to live in Costa Rica with kids in 2026: Hacienda Pinilla, Reserva Conchal, Flamingo, Potrero and Tamarindo, with nearby international schools and a family moving checklist.
body:
**If you are moving to Costa Rica with kids, the best areas to live in 2026 are Hacienda Pinilla, Reserva Conchal, and Flamingo and Potrero, with Tamarindo as the pick for families who want to walk to everything.** Each one sits close to at least one established international school, and that single fact matters more than the house, the view, or the price.

I am Tiago Leao, a real estate agent with KRAIN in Guanacaste. My family moved to Costa Rica 15 years ago, I grew up on these beaches, and I graduated from CRIA, one of the schools in this guide, five years ago. So when parents ask me where to live, I am answering as someone who did the school run here, not just someone who sells houses here.

If you came here from my video, this is the full guide I promised. If you want help with your specific family, [message me on WhatsApp](https://wa.me/50683028660) with your kids' ages and I will tell you where I would look.

## Start with the school, not the house

Every family I work with asks about the house first. Within a week, they are asking about the school first. Here is why, and it is the most important thing in this entire guide:

**The school decides the town. The town decides the commute. The commute decides which houses are even worth seeing.**

A few things that surprise almost every parent:

- **There are no school ratings here.** No GreatSchools, no state test scores, no independent body ranking schools on a comparable scale. Anyone showing you a score for a Costa Rican school made it up. The visit is the research.
- **Most schools run a bus.** Many of the international schools offer morning and afternoon transport, which can save you the daily drive. Before you pick a neighborhood, ask each school where its routes go and whether they pass your area.
- **The good schools have waitlists.** Grades 6 through 9 are the tightest. Families who arrive in July expecting to sort school out in August can find nothing available until the following February.
- **A school 12 km away is not 12 minutes away.** Roads bend around rivers and hills, and in the rainy months some of them get slow. Drive the route at 7am on a weekday before you buy.

The full breakdown of every school on this coast, with curriculum, grades and accreditation, is in my [guide to schools in Guanacaste](/blog/schools-guanacaste-gold-coast-guide/). You can also browse [every school profile](/schools.html) on my site.

## 1. Hacienda Pinilla

Hacienda Pinilla is where we sell more homes than anywhere else on this coast, and families are a big reason why.

It is a large gated beach and golf community on the coast just south of Tamarindo. It includes:

- **Gated, controlled access**, which is the first thing most relocating parents ask about
- **Multiple beaches**, including Playa Avellanas, one of Guanacaste's best-known surf breaks, plus Mansita and Bonita inside the resort
- **A beachfront Beach Club**
- **An 18-hole golf course**, tennis and pickleball
- **Mountain bike and hiking trails** through tropical dry forest
- **An equestrian center**
- **Tons of open space**, which is the part kids actually care about

**For school:** there is a bus that picks kids up inside Hacienda Pinilla every morning and takes them to [CRIA](/school/costa-rica-international-academy/). A lot of my classmates rode that bus every day, and it saved their parents the drive. Pinilla is also close to Tamarindo, home to [TIDE Academy](/school/tide-academy/), a small school of around 80 students from 17 countries with an 8:1 student-teacher ratio, and [Journey School](/school/journey-school-tamarindo/), an IB World School running Pre-K through 12, is about a 12-minute drive from Tamarindo.

**Best for:** families who want space, security and an outdoor life, and do not mind driving into Tamarindo for school and errands.

**Keep in mind:** Pinilla is organized into separate neighborhoods, each with its own fees and rules. Two similar homes can carry very different monthly costs. Get the fee schedule for the specific section in writing.

More detail is in my [Hacienda Pinilla guide](/blog/hacienda-pinilla-communities-amenities-guide/) and on my [Hacienda Pinilla community page](/development/hacienda-pinilla/).

## 2. Reserva Conchal

Reserva Conchal is the most complete master-planned community on this coast, and it is the one with the strongest school story of all.

It rises behind Playa Conchal, the crushed-shell beach between Brasilito and Flamingo. You get:

- **A private gated community** with controlled access
- **The beach**, with a private Beach Club right on Playa Conchal
- **A championship golf course**
- **Trails and restaurants**, plus the Westin and the W operating inside the gates
- **Seventeen residential communities**, from condos and townhomes to custom homes and lots

**For school:** [Costa Rica International Academy (CRIA)](/school/costa-rica-international-academy/) is basically right outside, about 500 meters from the entrance. It is U.S.-accredited and bilingual, sits on a 32-acre campus, and has been running since 2000, which makes it one of the longest-established international schools on the coast.

I graduated from CRIA five years ago and had a great experience there. I am not a neutral observer on this one, and I will not pretend to be.

**Best for:** families who want amenities managed for them, a U.S.-track education, and the shortest school run on this list.

**Keep in mind:** living inside a working resort, with hotels inside the gates, is exactly the appeal for some families and a deal-breaker for others. Each of the seventeen communities also has its own fees, so compare them carefully.

More in my [Reserva Conchal guide](/blog/reserva-conchal-real-estate-communities-guide/) and on my [Reserva Conchal community page](/development/reserva-conchal/).

## 3. Flamingo and Potrero

If Pinilla and Conchal are resort living, Flamingo and Potrero are a real beach town. For a lot of families, that is the whole point.

You get a quieter beach-town lifestyle, the Flamingo Marina, restaurants, grocery stores, and a year-round community that keeps growing. The two towns sit next to each other and feel different:

- **Flamingo** has the white-sand showpiece beach, the marina, and hillside homes with big ocean views.
- **Potrero** wraps a calm, protected bay. The water is the swimmable, paddleable kind, which matters a lot more than people expect when your kids are small. It is also where your money goes furthest on this stretch of coast.

### Mar Vista, the one to know about

Tucked on the hillside between Brasilito and Flamingo is **Mar Vista**, a master-planned community built around a clubhouse with an infinity pool, the Gracia restaurant, tennis and pickleball courts, and hiking and biking trails.

Here is why families should know the name: [La Paz Community School's Cabo Velas campus](/school/la-paz-community-school-cabo-velas/) sits right at Mar Vista's entrance. That makes it the only large community on this coast with an accredited international school at its gate. La Paz is an IB World School, PreK through 12, with dual-language immersion.

If a walkable or near-walkable school run is your dream, this is about as close as it gets here. More in my [Mar Vista guide](/blog/mar-vista-flamingo-real-estate-guide/) and on my [Mar Vista community page](/development/mar-vista/).

**For school:** La Paz is very close to Flamingo and Potrero, and CRIA is a short drive south by Conchal. Having two strong, different schools nearby gives you a real choice, which not every area can offer.

**Best for:** families who want a genuine town instead of a gated resort, calm water for little kids, and a community of people who actually live here year-round.

**Keep in mind:** Flamingo's hills mean driving to the beach and dinner. Potrero has fewer amenities than the resort communities today.

For the side-by-side comparison, read [Flamingo vs Conchal vs Potrero](/blog/flamingo-vs-conchal-vs-potrero-real-estate/), and see my [Flamingo](/flamingo.html) and [Potrero](/potrero.html) town pages.

## Bonus: Tamarindo, if you want to walk to everything

Tamarindo did not make my top three for one reason: it is busy. But for some families that energy is exactly right, so it belongs in this guide.

It is the most developed town on the coast. Restaurants, surf schools, shops and services are all close together, and in parts of town you really can walk to the beach and to dinner. It also has the most school options within a short drive:

- [Journey School](/school/journey-school-tamarindo/), IB World School, Pre-K through 12, about a 12-minute drive from Tamarindo
- [TIDE Academy](/school/tide-academy/), small, personalized, and deliberately different
- [Educarte](/school/educarte/), bilingual and MEP-certified, also about a 12-minute drive from Tamarindo, and the only school on this coast that publishes its tuition

Newer communities on the hillside, like [Tamarindo Park](/blog/tamarindo-park-real-estate-buyers-guide/) and [Senderos](/blog/senderos-tamarindo-real-estate-guide/), give you more space while staying close to town.

**Best for:** families with teenagers who want independence, parents who hate driving, and anyone who wants a lively town.

**Keep in mind:** the same energy that makes Tamarindo fun makes it louder and busier, especially in high season. More on the [Tamarindo town page](/tamarindo.html).

## Which area fits your family?

- **You want space, security and nature:** Hacienda Pinilla
- **You want a U.S.-accredited school minutes away and everything managed for you:** Reserva Conchal
- **You want an IB school at your gate:** Mar Vista in Flamingo
- **You want a real town and calm water for small kids:** Potrero
- **You want to walk to things and have the most school choices:** Tamarindo

## What else to know before you move

### Choosing a curriculum

If there is any chance your kids will finish school somewhere else, **IB travels best.** On this stretch of coast that means Journey and La Paz. If you want a U.S.-track education, CRIA is the anchor. If there is any chance your kids stay in the Costa Rican system, ask every school directly about **MEP accreditation**, which is what makes a diploma valid here.

### Healthcare for the kids

If you get residency, you enroll in CAJA, the public healthcare system. Once the primary applicant is enrolled, **a spouse and children under 18 are covered at no additional cost.** Many families also carry private insurance or pay out of pocket at private clinics for speed and choice.

### Residency covers the whole family

You do not need a separate application for every child. **One qualifying applicant can include a spouse and dependent children.** I went through residency myself as a dependent when my family moved here. The full breakdown of the three main paths is in my [residency guide](/blog/costa-rica-residency-property-buyers/).

### Rent before you buy

Americans and Canadians can stay up to 180 days on a tourist entry. Use that time. Rent in the area you are leaning toward, enroll the kids if you can, and live through a rainy season before you commit to a house. My [guide to moving to Costa Rica](/blog/moving-to-costa-rica-buyers-guide/) walks through the whole move in the order that actually works.

### A realistic order of operations

1. Pick two or three schools based on curriculum, not on the town you liked on vacation.
2. Call them and ask about openings in your kid's exact grade for your exact start date.
3. Visit every one in person.
4. Drive the route from the areas you are considering, at 7am on a weekday.
5. Then start looking at homes.

Families who do it in this order settle in. Families who buy the house first are often back on the market within two years.

## Tell me about your family

I grew up here, I went to school here, and I know which drives look fine on a map and are miserable at 7am. Send me a message and I will help you narrow this down to the right area for your kids.

It helps if you tell me:

1. **Your kids' ages and grades**
2. **The school or curriculum you are leaning toward**, even if you are not sure yet
3. **Your rough budget**, and whether you want to rent first or buy
4. **When you are hoping to move**

I answer every message myself, in English, Spanish or Portuguese.

**[Message me on WhatsApp](https://wa.me/50683028660)**, or email [tiago@soldbytiago.com](mailto:tiago@soldbytiago.com). You can also browse [current listings](/properties.html) near all of these schools.

*This guide is general information. Amenities, fees, school availability, bus routes, enrollment and immigration rules change, so confirm current details directly with the community, the school and a licensed Costa Rican immigration attorney.*

## FAQ

### What is the best area in Costa Rica to live with kids?

On the Guanacaste, the strongest areas for families are Hacienda Pinilla, Reserva Conchal, and Flamingo and Potrero, with Tamarindo for families who want walkability. The right one depends on which school you choose, because the school run shapes daily life more than any other factor.

### Are there good international schools in Guanacaste?

Yes. Established options include CRIA, a U.S.-accredited bilingual school next to Reserva Conchal; La Paz Community School, an IB World School at the entrance to Mar Vista in Flamingo; and TIDE Academy in Tamarindo, with Journey School about a 12-minute drive away. There are no official school ratings in Costa Rica, so visiting in person is the real research.

### Is Hacienda Pinilla good for families?

For families who want space and security, yes. It is gated, has multiple beaches, a Beach Club, trails, golf, tennis and an equestrian center, and a bus picks kids up inside the community every morning and takes them to CRIA. It is also close to Tamarindo's schools, including TIDE Academy and Journey School.

### Which school is near Reserva Conchal?

Costa Rica International Academy (CRIA) is about 500 meters from the Reserva Conchal entrance. It is U.S.-accredited and bilingual and has operated since 2000.

### Do kids get healthcare in Costa Rica?

Residents enroll in CAJA, Costa Rica's public healthcare system, and once the primary applicant is enrolled, a spouse and children under 18 are covered at no additional cost. Many families add private insurance as well.

### When should I start looking at schools before moving?

Before you choose a town, and ideally months ahead of your move. Waitlists are real, especially for grades 6 through 9, and families who wait until they arrive can find no openings until the following school term.

## About the author

Tiago Leao is a real estate agent with KRAIN Luxury Real Estate in Guanacaste, working Tamarindo, Hacienda Pinilla, Playa Grande, Flamingo, Potrero, Brasilito and Conchal. His family moved to Costa Rica 15 years ago; he grew up on this coast, went through residency as a dependent, and graduated from CRIA. He works in English, Spanish and Portuguese. Reach him on [WhatsApp](https://wa.me/50683028660).

title: Schools in Guanacaste: A Guide for Relocating Families
excerpt: Every international, bilingual and private school in Guanacaste — IB, Montessori, Waldorf and bilingual — plus the things that actually decide it: the drive, the waitlist, and why there are no school ratings in Costa Rica.
meta_desc: A guide to international and bilingual schools in Guanacaste, Costa Rica — Journey, La Paz, CRIA, Del Mar, TIDE and more. Grades, curriculum and what relocating families need to know.
body:
Almost every family that calls me about moving to Guanacaste asks about the house first and the school second. Within a week, it has flipped. The school decides the town, the town decides the commute, and the commute decides which houses are even worth seeing.

So here is the honest version of what exists in Guanacaste, and what nobody tells you until you are already here.

## First, the thing that surprises everyone

There is no GreatSchools here.

If you are coming from the US, you are used to opening a listing and seeing a 6/10 next to every nearby school. That number comes from state standardized testing. Costa Rica has no equivalent, and no independent body rates these schools on a comparable scale.

This matters more than it sounds. It means **anyone showing you a school score for Costa Rica invented it.** I would rather tell you what each school says about itself and let you do the visit than hand you a number I made up.

That is why the [schools page](https://soldbytiago.com/schools.html) on this site has no ratings. Grades, curriculum, languages, accreditation. Nothing else.

## The schools, by town

### Tamarindo and just inland

**[Journey School of Costa Rica](https://soldbytiago.com/school.html?slug=journey-school-tamarindo)** — Pre-K through 12, and an authorized IB World School, which is the credential most relocating families are scanning for. Also accredited through Middle States and part of the UNESCO Associated Schools Network.

**[TIDE Academy](https://soldbytiago.com/school.html?slug=tide-academy)** — the outlier, and deliberately so. Around 80 students from 17 countries at an 8:1 student-teacher ratio, built for kids whose interests run past a conventional academic structure. They publish very little about grades or curriculum, which tells you something about how they operate. Go see it.

**[Educarte](https://soldbytiago.com/school.html?slug=educarte)** — bilingual, MEP-certified, out toward Huacas. It is also the only school on this entire list that publishes its tuition: **$125 per month** for preschool and primary. Every other school on the coast makes you ask.

**[Pacífico Internacional](https://soldbytiago.com/school.html?slug=pacifico-internacional)** — Waldorf-inspired, preschool through middle school, up in the hills at Cañafistula. If Waldorf is your thing, this is the only option on this coast.

### Flamingo, Brasilito and Conchal

**[La Paz Community School — Cabo Velas](https://soldbytiago.com/school.html?slug=la-paz-community-school-cabo-velas)** — IB World School, PreK–12, dual-language immersion, sitting between Flamingo and Brasilito. Also accredited with ACEP and College Board. For a lot of families buying in Flamingo or Potrero, La Paz is the reason.

**[Costa Rica International Academy (CRIA)](https://soldbytiago.com/school.html?slug=costa-rica-international-academy)** — US-accredited and bilingual, on a 32-acre campus 500m south of Reserva Conchal. Founded in 2000, which makes it one of the longest-running international schools on the coast. If you want a US-track education, this is the anchor.

### Playas del Coco and the north

**[Dolphin's Academy](https://soldbytiago.com/school.html?slug=dolphins-academy)** — bilingual elementary in Coco, with curricula developed in alliance with Oxford and Cambridge.

**[Lakeside International School](https://soldbytiago.com/school.html?slug=lakeside-international-school)** — PreK–12, bilingual, inland at Tablazo de Sardinal, built around an integrated Multiple Intelligences curriculum.

**[La Paz — Tempisque Campus](https://soldbytiago.com/school.html?slug=la-paz-community-school-tempisque)** — La Paz's second campus, inland near Palmira in Carrillo, running the same IB dual-language program as Cabo Velas. Worth knowing about if you are looking around Papagayo.

### Nosara

**[Del Mar Academy](https://soldbytiago.com/school.html?slug=del-mar-academy)** — Pre-K through 12 on an 11-acre campus, running Montessori in the early years and finishing with the IB Diploma. Nosara is its own world, and Del Mar is a real part of why families commit to it.

## What actually decides this

### The drive is the whole thing

A school 12 km away is not 12 minutes away. Roads here bend around rivers, hills and the occasional herd of cattle, and in October some of them are worse than that. Families who skip this end up doing 50 minutes each way, twice a day, and they do not last.

**Drive it before you buy.** At 7am on a weekday, in the rain if you can manage it. Not at noon on a Sunday.

### Most schools run a bus

Most of the international schools on this coast offer morning and afternoon bus routes, which can save you the daily drive. Hacienda Pinilla, for example, has a bus that picks kids up inside the community every morning and takes them to CRIA, and plenty of families rely on it. Routes do not reach everywhere, though, so ask each school where its buses go before you choose a neighborhood.

### IB is the export ticket

If there is any chance your kid finishes high school somewhere else, IB travels. On this coast that means Journey, La Paz (both campuses), and Del Mar. Not the only good option, but the one that keeps doors open.

### The waitlist is real

The good schools fill. Grades 6 through 9 are the tightest. Families arrive in July assuming they will sort school out in August and find nothing available until the following February.

**Call the schools before you shortlist towns.** Not after.

### MEP matters more than you think

MEP is Costa Rica's Ministry of Education. MEP accreditation is what makes a diploma valid here. If there is any chance of your kid staying in the Costa Rican system, or of you needing local paperwork to line up cleanly, ask about MEP status directly.

## How to actually do this

1. Pick two or three schools based on curriculum, not on which town you liked on vacation.
2. Call them. Ask about openings in your kid's exact grade for your exact start date.
3. Visit. All of them. In person. There is no rating to lean on, so the visit is the research.
4. Drive the route from the neighborhoods you are considering, at the hour you would actually drive it.
5. Then look at houses.

Families who do it in this order settle in. Families who buy the house first tend to be back on the market within two years, and I have listed a few of those.

## Where I come in

Every listing on this site shows the schools nearest to it, with distances. That is straight-line distance, so treat it as a starting point rather than a commute estimate.

If you tell me which school you are aiming at, I can work backwards to the neighborhoods that make that drive tolerable. That is usually a much shorter list than people expect, and it is a far more useful place to start than a price filter.

I grew up on this coast. I know which drives look fine on a map and are miserable in practice. Reach out at [tiago@soldbytiago.com](mailto:tiago@soldbytiago.com) and tell me the ages of your kids.

---

*Details on this page come from each school's own published materials as of July 2026. Programs, tuition and accreditation change. Confirm everything directly with the school before you make a decision this size.*

## From school choice to home choice

I help families compare communities against the daily logistics of a school run - real drive times, not map distances - and build a housing shortlist around them. Admissions, tuition and enrollment should always be confirmed directly with each school; when available, I can point you to the right admissions contact.

title: The Best Golf Communities in Costa Rica: Where to Buy on the Guanacaste Coast
excerpt: Hacienda Pinilla, Reserva Conchal and the Papagayo Peninsula: the three places on the Guanacaste coast where you can own a home and play championship golf — what golf access really costs, and why these communities suit non-golfers just as well.
meta_desc: The best golf communities in Costa Rica for 2026: Hacienda Pinilla, Reserva Conchal and the Papagayo Peninsula, with club access, fees and what they offer non-golfers, from a local agent.
body:
**If golf is a priority when you buy in Costa Rica, three places on the Guanacaste coast are worth your time: Hacienda Pinilla, Reserva Conchal, and the Papagayo Peninsula.** They are the communities where you can own a home and play championship golf without getting in the car, and they are not interchangeable — they differ in how you own the land, what the club membership actually gives you, and how much of the year the course stays busy.

And if you are reading this for a partner who plays while you would rather be on the beach: all three are worth your time too. The course is the reason these communities are the best-maintained places on this coast, and most of what that buys you has nothing to do with golf. There is a section on that below.

I am Tiago Leao, a real estate agent with KRAIN in Guanacaste. If you came here from my video, this is the full version I promised. If you want help with your specific situation, [message me on WhatsApp](https://wa.me/50683028660) and tell me your budget and how often you would actually play — that answer moves people between these three faster than anything else.

## First, the thing that catches most buyers out

Buying a house inside a golf community does not automatically make you a member of the golf club.

In Costa Rica, the home and the club are usually two separate things. The property is one purchase; access to the course is a membership, a resident rate, a transferable right, or nothing at all, depending on the community, the section you buy in, and sometimes the individual unit. I have seen buyers assume that a golf-course view means golf privileges, and find out at closing that the membership is a separate cost, or that it did not transfer from the seller.

So before you fall for a house, make sure you know three things:

- Whether any club or golf right conveys with this specific property, and whether it transfers to a future buyer
- The current cost: initiation or transfer fee, annual dues, cart and green fees at the resident rate
- Whether your guests and tenants can play, and at what rate — this matters enormously if you plan to rent

Everything below assumes you are going to ask those questions. The rest is what makes each place different.

## 1. Hacienda Pinilla

![The Hacienda Pinilla golf course running out to the Pacific, south of Tamarindo in Guanacaste, Costa Rica](/golf-hacienda-pinilla.jpg)

An 18-hole championship course designed by Mike Young that plays to par 72 at up to roughly 7,200 yards, holding an Audubon Cooperative Sanctuary designation for its conservation practices. The routing runs through 4,500 acres of gated coastal land and out toward the Pacific, with about three miles of coastline inside the property.

What makes Pinilla the strongest option for most golf buyers is simple: there are real residential neighborhoods built directly around the course, not just near it. Reserva de Golf, for example, is a defined 136-lot neighborhood along the fairways. You can buy a lot on the course and build, buy an existing golf-course home, or buy a condo and still be minutes from the first tee.

The rest of the community backs it up — a beachfront Beach Club, an equestrian center, tennis and pickleball, mountain-bike and hiking trails through dry forest, a small market, and the JW Marriott operating inside the gates. Ownership here is the ordinary kind that foreign buyers are used to, which keeps the legal side straightforward — your attorney confirms exactly how your specific property is held.

**It fits** the buyer who wants to genuinely live in a golf community, wants the beach five minutes from the course, and wants a range of price points to choose from rather than one narrow band. It also fits families who will never touch a club — the trails, the beaches, the equestrian center and the quiet streets are the reason plenty of my buyers here chose it.

Pinilla is where we sell more homes than anywhere else on this coast. My agent's view of the neighborhoods, plus current listings inside the resort, is on the [Hacienda Pinilla community page](/development/hacienda-pinilla/), and the deeper write-up is in my [Hacienda Pinilla guide](/blog/hacienda-pinilla-communities-amenities-guide/).

## 2. Reserva Conchal

![A golfer teeing off over the water on the Robert Trent Jones II course at Reserva Conchal, Guanacaste, Costa Rica](/golf-reserva-conchal.jpg)

An 18-hole championship course designed by Robert Trent Jones II, also certified as an Audubon sanctuary, inside roughly 2,300 acres behind Playa Conchal's crushed-shell beach.

The trade here is golf plus a fully managed resort environment. The private Beach Club sits directly on Conchal. Restaurants, landscaping, security and infrastructure are all handled to a resort standard, and two international hotels — the all-inclusive Westin and the W Costa Rica — operate inside the same gates. The community also runs an unusual sustainability setup for this coast, including renewable energy, on-site water treatment, and desalination, which is worth understanding in detail in a region where water is the real long-term question.

Residentially it is the most varied of the three: seventeen named communities ranging from golf-view condominiums through townhomes and custom homes to building lots, each with its own character, administration and fee structure. That variety is the strength here — there is a version of Conchal at most price points — and it means the section you choose is worth understanding as carefully as the house itself.

**It fits** the buyer who wants golf and the beach handed to them without managing anything, and who likes having a resort's restaurants and service on the doorstep. Non-golfers do well here for the same reason: the Beach Club, the restaurants and the landscaping are maintained to the same standard as the course.

More detail in my [Reserva Conchal guide](/blog/reserva-conchal-real-estate-communities-guide/), and if you are weighing this stretch of coast generally, [Flamingo vs Conchal vs Potrero](/blog/flamingo-vs-conchal-vs-potrero-real-estate/) is the comparison I send most often.

## 3. The Papagayo Peninsula

![An ocean-view hole on the Papagayo Peninsula, Guanacaste, Costa Rica, with the Gulf of Papagayo and its islands beyond](/golf-papagayo.jpg)

The most luxurious of the three, and the most specialized. The Ocean Course is an Arnold Palmer Signature design with ocean views from 14 of its holes, set on a peninsula in the Gulf of Papagayo surrounded by some of the highest-end real estate in the country, with the Four Seasons and Andaz nearby and Liberia airport the closest of any community here.

It is also the most private setting of the three: a peninsula of headlands, coves and protected forest, with hotel-grade service, marina access and beaches that most people never see. Ownership works differently from property to property here, so one of the first things I do on a Papagayo home is walk you through exactly how that one is held and what comes with it.

**It fits** the buyer at the top of the market who wants resort-grade everything, the shortest airport run, and the most dramatic golf of the three — and the non-golfer at that level, who is really buying the setting, the privacy and the hotels. Inventory is small and tightly held, so the right property tends to be found rather than shopped — worth starting the search early.

## What these communities give you if you never play

I sell plenty of homes in these three to people who do not own a set of clubs, and the reasoning is always some version of the same thing: a golf course is an expensive thing to keep alive in a dry climate, so a community that maintains one to championship standard maintains everything else too.

What that actually means day to day:

- **Roads, landscaping and security that stay maintained.** The same crews and the same budget cover the whole property, which is why these communities look the same in October as they do in February.
- **Open space that will not be built on.** A course is 150-odd acres of permanent green in the middle of a community, plus the trees, wildlife corridors and quiet edges that come with it. In a market where the lot next door can become a construction site, that is worth real money.
- **Somewhere to go on foot or by bike.** Wide, low-traffic streets, trails, and a clubhouse restaurant that works as a neighborhood bar for people who never tee off.
- **The rest of the amenities.** Between these three you get beaches and beach clubs, tennis and pickleball, gyms, pools, restaurants, an equestrian center and hotels inside the gates.
- **Resale and rental demand.** Golfers are a small share of buyers but a reliable one, and a golf address widens the pool of people who want your house later. Guests book them for the setting as much as the tee times.

What you are paying for, through the dues, is exactly that standard of upkeep and that open space — so know the monthly number going in and decide what it is worth to you. For a lot of my non-golfing buyers, it is the reason they chose one of these three over anywhere else on the coast.

## What to know before you make an offer

Golf communities layer a club, a master association and a section association on top of each other, and each one has its own costs and rules. Before you offer:

1. Make sure you know the dues — the club, the section and the master resort — so the monthly number you are working with is the real one.
2. Know what golf access comes with the property, what it costs, and whether it passes to the next owner.
3. Know the section's rental rules if you plan to rent, including whether your guests can use the club and the course.
4. Ask about the association's reserves and anything already planned for the year ahead.
5. Run the standard checks that apply to any purchase here: [due diligence](/blog/costa-rica-property-due-diligence-checklist/), the [water letter](/blog/costa-rica-property-water-letter-guide/), and [title and plano](/blog/costa-rica-property-title-plano-catastrado-guide/).

## How I would choose between the three

Three questions usually settle it.

**How often will you really play?** Every week, and you want the course out your door: Pinilla. A handful of rounds between beach days: Conchal, where the Beach Club carries the rest of the week.

**Do you want to manage anything?** No: Conchal. Somewhat: Pinilla. Not the question you are asking: Papagayo.

**Who else is coming?** Kids and non-golfing partners usually decide this one. Pinilla spreads out across beaches, trails and an equestrian center; Conchal keeps everyone inside one managed resort; Papagayo is the quietest and the most grown-up of the three.

## Ready to look?

Tell me your budget, how often you would play, and whether this is a full-time home, a second home or a rental, and I will tell you which of the three I would put you in and what is currently available. [Message me on WhatsApp](https://wa.me/50683028660) — I answer every message myself, in English, Spanish or Portuguese — or browse [every current listing](/properties.html) on the site.

Course details above are what the clubs currently publish, and access terms change — I check the current terms for whichever property you are looking at.

title: The Best Surf Beaches to Live and Buy in Costa Rica
excerpt: Playa Avellanas, Playa Grande and Marbella: where to buy on the Guanacaste coast if you surf — the spots, the tides and the crowds at each one, and how each town handles the rest of the family.
meta_desc: The best surf towns in Costa Rica to live and buy property in 2026: Playa Avellanas and Hacienda Pinilla, Playa Grande and Marbella, from a local agent who grew up surfing them.
body:
**If you surf and you are buying property in Costa Rica, three places on the Guanacaste coast are worth your time in 2026: Playa Avellanas, Playa Grande, and Marbella.** All three put you within minutes of serious waves, and they are very different places to live — one gated and full of amenities, one protected and low-density, one still wide open.

I am Tiago Leao, a real estate agent with KRAIN in Guanacaste. I have surfed for the past 15 years of my life and grew up surfing every one of these beaches, so when someone tells me what they ride and how often they want to be in the water, I can usually name the town before we talk about houses. If you came here from my video, this is the full guide I promised — and if you want help with your own search, [message me on WhatsApp](https://wa.me/50683028660).

## Buy for the Tuesday, not the swell of the year

Every surf town here looks perfect on the day you visit. The question that actually matters is what an ordinary Tuesday looks like: is there a rideable wave when the swell is average, can you get to it in ten minutes, and is it a wave you want at your level?

Three things decide that, and they are worth settling before you look at a single listing:

- **Consistency.** Some of these beaches work almost every day of the year; others need swell. If you plan to surf several times a week, consistency beats perfection.
- **How close you really are.** A house ten minutes from the peak gets surfed; a house forty minutes away gets surfed on weekends. Time the drive from the actual property, not from the town sign.
- **Who else is going in the water.** If your family is learning, you want a beach with a soft inside section, not only a heavy outer reef.

## 1. Playa Avellanas

![Golden morning light on a clean wave at Playa Avellanas, Guanacaste, Costa Rica](/surf-avellanas.jpg)

Avellanas is one of Costa Rica's legendary surf beaches and it has kept its character: mangrove boardwalk, boards in the back of the truck, lunch at Lola's. The dirt road in is being paved right now, which makes the daily drive easier and is worth knowing if you are watching values on this stretch.

There are three main setups along the beach, and they cover every level between them.

- **Little Hawaii** is the right point break at the north end, breaking right in front of the Hacienda Pinilla Beach Club. There is rock underneath and it works on basically all tides. Unless it is really big it is not a strong wave, which is part of why people love it.
- **The river mouth** goes both ways and works on all tides, though mid tide is my favorite. It is a bit rocky, and there is one big rock head that pops out on the left — know where it is before you paddle out.
- **Lola's and Dead Tree**, at the south end, is a beach break that is best at high tide. On a smaller day it is perfect for kids.

What makes Avellanas unusual is that you get two completely different ways to live next to the same wave. You can buy in the laid-back beach town, or you can buy inside [Hacienda Pinilla](/development/hacienda-pinilla/) — 4,500 gated acres with an 18-hole golf course, a private beach club, an equestrian center, trails, the JW Marriott, and Journey School operating inside the gates. From either one you are in the lineup in about ten minutes, and Tamarindo is about 25 minutes up the road when you want a night out.

So one beach covers the whole household: the south end for kids and anyone learning, the river mouth and Little Hawaii for the more advanced surfers in the family when there is swell.

**It fits** the surfer who wants amenities, schools and security within the gates, or the family where one person surfs every morning and everyone else wants a beach club and a golf course. More in my [Avellanas and Hacienda Pinilla guide](/avellanas.html).

## 2. Playa Grande

![A surfer deep in a clean barrel at Playa Grande, Guanacaste, Costa Rica](/surf-playa-grande.jpg)

If surfing is the main priority, this would probably be my pick.

Grande is the most reliable wave of the three. It has good waves year round, whatever the size, as long as you go at high tide or close to it — that is the one rule here. Time it right and there is something to surf; the only days it really falls apart are when it gets too big and goes messy.

It is faster, hollower and more powerful than Tamarindo directly across the estuary, and on the right days you get proper A-frames and barrels. The main peak is crowded and there are a lot of locals in the water, but the beach runs for more than a kilometer, so finding your own empty peak is easy. My two picks are far right, close to the rock, and the main peak in front of Taco Star.

The town lives by different rules from its neighbors, and that is the appeal. The beach is part of Las Baulas National Park, one of the world's most important leatherback nesting sites, which means low-density zoning, dark skies at night, and a permanent ceiling on how big Playa Grande can ever get. The wave you buy for will still be the wave in twenty years, and so will the emptiness. There is a small core of good restaurants, a market, surf shops and boutique hotels, and Tamarindo's full amenities are a two-minute boat ride across the estuary.

**It fits** the surfer who wants the best everyday wave in the Tamarindo area, and the buyer who likes knowing the town cannot be built out around them. More in my [Playa Grande guide](/playa-grande.html), and if you are weighing it against town life, [Tamarindo vs Playa Grande](/blog/tamarindo-vs-playa-grande-real-estate/) is the comparison I send most often.

## 3. Marbella

![A clean wave peeling at Marbella on the Guanacaste coast, Costa Rica, with a surfer walking down the empty beach](/surf-marbella.jpg)

Marbella is the stretch most people drive past, between Avellanas and Nosara. It is the least consistent of the three, and that is the whole trade: you wait, and when it comes together you get the barrel of a lifetime. A busy day is a handful of people in the water.

Tides split the coast here — the north side is best from low to mid tide, the south side from mid to high — so there is usually somewhere to go when there is swell running. South toward San Juanillo and north toward Junquillal, the coves and points keep coming, and this is still the largest stretch of underexplored surf coast left in Guanacaste.

It is also where the value is. Land here sits at prices the bigger towns have not seen in fifteen years. The road was just fixed, so getting in and out is no longer the ordeal it used to be: about an hour north to Tamarindo, about an hour south to Nosara. The village has the basics you need to live here, though it is smaller than the other two towns, and Starlink, fiber and solar cover the rest.

**It fits** the surfer who wants perfect waves whenever swell shows up, likes a quieter and more self-sufficient life, and wants more coastline and more house for the money. More in my [Marbella guide](/marbella.html).

## If you surf and the rest of the family does not

This is most of my surf buyers, and it is worth planning for. The person who is in the water at six in the morning is easy to please. Everyone else needs the rest of the day to work.

- **Avellanas and Hacienda Pinilla** handle this best. Golf, a beach club, tennis, trails, an equestrian center and a school inside the gates mean nobody is waiting around for the surfer to come in.
- **Playa Grande** is the nature-first version: turtle season on the same sand, dark skies, empty beach walks, and Tamarindo minutes away by boat when you want restaurants and shops.
- **Marbella** suits the household that genuinely wants the quiet, with Nosara's yoga, restaurants and schools about an hour south when you want more.

If school runs are part of the picture, my [family guide](/blog/best-places-to-live-costa-rica-with-kids/) covers which schools each of these areas feeds into, and if golf is also in the mix, [the golf communities guide](/blog/best-golf-communities-costa-rica/) covers the overlap — Hacienda Pinilla is on both lists for a reason.

## Practical things that make a surf house work

1. Time the walk or drive from the property to the peak you would actually surf, at the hour you would actually go.
2. Learn the tide each spot wants. Grande needs high tide, Avellanas works through most of them, and Marbella splits north and south. It changes what time of day you actually surf.
3. Check the access road in green season, especially further out. It decides how often you go.
4. Look at water, power and internet early on the quieter stretches, where solar, wells and Starlink are normal rather than unusual.
5. If you plan to rent it out, a surf address rents itself — the closer and more walkable it is to the beach, the easier the calendar fills.

## How I would choose between the three

**Surfing every single day?** Playa Grande, because it has something on it year round at high tide. Marbella if you would rather wait for perfect and have it to yourself.

**Family coming with you?** Avellanas and Hacienda Pinilla, where the amenities and the school do the heavy lifting.

**Want the most coastline for your money?** Marbella, while it is still early there.
